newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico phone union wants new members, no jobs lost.
newsitem.headline: Mexico phone union wants new members, no jobs lost.

text.p: Mexico's combative telephone workers' leader, Francisco Hernandez Juarez, said he is considering pushing for unionization in new telephone companies that will begin competing with current monopoly holder Telefonos de Mexico in 1997.

"At the moment we are not campaigning for workers from other companies, but not because we don't think there are possibilities. We will look at that option as a second stage," Hernandez said in an interview with Reuters.
Hernandez said his current priority was to prevent job cuts at Telefonos de Mexico (Telmex) as it faces up to competition.
"Our priority for now is to consolidate the workforce at Telmex, that modernization in the face of competition should take place without laying off workers," he said.
"Job security for our members is vital for the very subsistence of the union," he added.
New companies will enter Mexico's long-distance telephone market when Telmex's monopoly ends on January 1, 1997.

Hernandez was reelected on Wednesday to serve another four-year term as secretary general of the Mexican Telephone Workers' Union (STRP). He is noted as being more independent than most Mexican labor union leaders of the Institutional Revolutionary Party, in power since 1929.
Hernandez foresaw problems arising next year over contending for collective employment contracts with the new companies that will compete with Telmex.
"All the new companies already have collective contracts, without having contracted a single worker, thereby attempting to avoid unionization problems," he said.
"Furthermore, they're following the anti-union policies of many transnationals," he added.
Hernandez also repeated recent suggestions that the STRP might leave the pro-government Congress of Labor union group.

"The Congress is anti-democratic, authoritarian and we want a more representative labor organization," he added, saying that the telephone workers were looking into setting up a new group along with the teachers' and electricians' unions, among others.
